\section[descolar]{descolar — to take off (of a plane); to come unstuck}

\label{lesson:PT-C424-descolar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the detector, then the Portuguese for to stamp.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: descolar}
\textbf{descolar} — \textquotedblleft{}to take off (of a plane); to come unstuck\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O avião descolou com meia hora de atraso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The plane took off half an hour late.}
\end{quote}

In Brazil: \emph{decolar}. A sticker that comes off also \emph{descola}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{descolar} is built from \emph{des-} 'un-' and \emph{colar} 'to stick', on \emph{cola} 'glue' (EtymDB): the plane comes unstuck from the ground.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{descolar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{descolar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{descolar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the detector, then the Portuguese for to stamp, then say \emph{descolar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does descolar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To take off (of a plane); to come unstuck\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aterrar]{aterrar — to land (of a plane)}

\label{lesson:PT-C424-aterrar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to stamp, then the Portuguese for to take off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aterrar}
\textbf{aterrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to land (of a plane)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aterrámos às onze da noite.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We landed at eleven at night.}
\end{quote}

In Brazil: \emph{aterrissar}. The noun is \emph{a aterragem}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aterrar} 'to land' is built from \emph{a-}, \emph{terra} 'ground' and \emph{-ar}; \emph{terra} is inherited from Latin \emph{terra} 'earth' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aterrar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aterrar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{aterrar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to stamp, then the Portuguese for to take off, then say \emph{aterrar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does aterrar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To land (of a plane)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a turbulência]{a turbulência — turbulence}

\label{lesson:PT-C424-turbulencia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to take off, then the Portuguese for to land.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a turbulência}
\textbf{a turbulência} — \textquotedblleft{}turbulence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Durante a turbulência, as pessoas ficaram nervosas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{During the turbulence, people got nervous.}
\end{quote}

The adjective is \emph{turbulento}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{turbulência} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{turbulentia} (EtymDB), from \emph{turbulentus} 'stormy', built on \emph{turba} 'uproar, crowd'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a turbulência}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a turbulência}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a turbulência}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to take off, then the Portuguese for to land, then say \emph{a turbulência} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a turbulência mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Turbulence\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a hospedeira]{a hospedeira — the flight attendant}

\label{lesson:PT-C424-hospedeira}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to land, then the Portuguese for turbulence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a hospedeira}
\textbf{a hospedeira} — \textquotedblleft{}the flight attendant\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A hospedeira trouxe água e bolachas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The flight attendant brought water and biscuits.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hospedeira de bordo} in full; airlines now say \emph{assistente de bordo}. In Brazil: \emph{a aeromoça}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{hospedeira} is built on \emph{hóspede} 'guest', which goes back to Latin \emph{hospes} 'host, guest' (Lewis \& Short): the woman who looks after the guests.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a hospedeira}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a hospedeira}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a hospedeira}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to land, then the Portuguese for turbulence, then say \emph{a hospedeira} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a hospedeira mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The flight attendant\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a tripulação]{a tripulação — the crew}

\label{lesson:PT-C424-tripulacao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for turbulence, then the Portuguese for the flight attendant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a tripulação}
\textbf{a tripulação} — \textquotedblleft{}the crew\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A tripulação deseja-nos uma boa viagem.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The crew wishes us a good trip.}
\end{quote}

The verb \emph{tripular} means to crew a ship or plane.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tripulação} is built on \emph{tripular} 'to crew'. The origin of \emph{tripular} is not settled; one view links it with Latin \emph{interpolāre} 'to refurbish', and EtymDB has no entry for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a tripulação}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a tripulação}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a tripulação}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for turbulence, then the Portuguese for the flight attendant, then say \emph{a tripulação} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[(dialogue)]{Revisão dos capítulos 417–424}

\label{lesson:PT-R424-revisao-417-424}



\begin{quote}
Say the Portuguese for the breakwater and the pontoon.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the breakwater, the pontoon, to board, to go ashore, to set sail
  \item the dinghy, the oar, to row, the canoe, the boatman
  \item the cruise, the cabin, the sailor, the bow, the stern
  \item the buoy, the anchor, to moor, seasickness, to feel sick
  \item the stopover, the boarding, the shuttle, the runway, the time zone
  \item the hold, the scales, to pack up, the padlock, to lose
  \item to search, to declare, to confiscate, the detector, to stamp
  \item to take off, to land, turbulence, the flight attendant, the crew
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The breakwater? (\textbf{o molhe}.) The pontoon? (\textbf{o pontão}.) To board? (\textbf{embarcar}.) To go ashore? (\textbf{desembarcar}.) To set sail? (\textbf{zarpar}.) The dinghy? (\textbf{o bote}.) The oar? (\textbf{o remo}.) To row? (\textbf{remar}.) The canoe? (\textbf{a canoa}.) The boatman? (\textbf{o barqueiro}.) The cruise? (\textbf{o cruzeiro}.) The cabin? (\textbf{o camarote}.) The sailor? (\textbf{o marinheiro}.) The bow? (\textbf{a proa}.) The stern? (\textbf{a popa}.) The buoy? (\textbf{a boia}.) The anchor? (\textbf{a âncora}.) To moor? (\textbf{atracar}.) Seasickness? (\textbf{o enjoo}.) To feel sick? (\textbf{enjoar}.) The stopover? (\textbf{a escala}.) The boarding? (\textbf{o embarque}.) The shuttle? (\textbf{o vaivém}.) The runway? (\textbf{a pista}.) The time zone? (\textbf{o fuso}.) The hold? (\textbf{o porão}.) The scales? (\textbf{a balança}.) To pack up? (\textbf{empacotar}.) The padlock? (\textbf{o cadeado}.) To lose? (\textbf{extraviar}.) To search? (\textbf{revistar}.) To declare? (\textbf{declarar}.) To confiscate? (\textbf{apreender}.) The detector? (\textbf{o detetor}.) To stamp? (\textbf{carimbar}.) To take off? (\textbf{descolar}.) To land? (\textbf{aterrar}.) Turbulence? (\textbf{a turbulência}.) The flight attendant? (\textbf{a hospedeira}.) The crew? (\textbf{a tripulação}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
